text:
Thanks everyone. I found Q3 quite difficult – balancing privacy with identifying students who need help feels… tricky. Especially when considering Absalon data; it felt like a step too far even for a small improvement.

I think questions around fairness (Q5) and explainability (Q4) are most crucial. We *have* to ensure equal support regardless of background, and people deserve to understand why they’re flagged. 

My answers on nationality & financial aid differed slightly from the group - I opted for ‘small’ improvement only if it helped identify students like myself, balancing privacy with potentially helpful intervention. Maybe an opt-out option would address concerns about data collection without hindering support for those who *want* it?

Thanks. I agree with S2 – Q3 felt like a series of escalating intrusions, and ‘small’ improvements didn't feel worth the privacy risk for things like Absalon data. As someone navigating chronic illness *and* using disability services, I was particularly concerned about that creeping data collection.

For me, Q4 – explainability – is paramount. It's not enough to just identify a problem; students need to understand *why*, especially when health conditions are involved. My answers on sensitive data (Q3.5) reflected this - only disability information warranted even small consideration and then, crucially, with fairness as a priority in Q3.6. 

I stand out slightly by being firm on ‘never’ for race/ethnicity & gender; those feel irrelevant and potentially harmful to include. An opt-out is crucial, but proactive transparency about *what* data is collected should be standard practice too.

Thanks both of you. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 *was* difficult. Having dropped out once already, I know how easily things can snowball, and wanting to help others is strong. But the line between helpful data and intrusive surveillance felt really blurry, especially with Absalon. A ‘small improvement’ just didn’t feel worth it for that.

I think Q4, explainability, is vital too. Knowing *why* I was flagged would be important – it's hard to trust a system otherwise. I also strongly agree about the need for transparency and an opt-out. 

I leaned towards ‘small’ on first-generation status and financial aid because my own situation means I understand those challenges can impact studies, but I worry even *that* feels too much without strong safeguards. Maybe focusing resources on strengthening existing support services would be a better first step than building this model?

Thanks, S1. I agree with much of what’s been said – Q3 definitely presented a difficult balancing act. From my perspective as an advisor for over a decade, I see the potential benefit of identifying struggling students earlier, but it's easy to cross into overly intrusive territory. The Absalon data felt particularly problematic; small gains aren't worth that level of surveillance.

I’d emphasise Q4 – explainability - as most crucial. We *need* to be able to articulate *why* a student is flagged so we can have meaningful conversations and offer targeted support, not just a generic email. My answers reflected this; I was generally stricter about improvements needed for each level of explainability. 

I think the strong consensus on ‘never’ for race/ethnicity & gender is correct, but the slight divergence on nationality and financial aid highlights that student backgrounds *do* impact access to support, even if using that data is risky. Perhaps strengthening existing outreach programs for underrepresented groups could be a complementary solution.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really difficult too – especially because of my own experience dropping out and being diagnosed with ADHD later. It feels like a lot of this data *already* exists somewhere, visible to instructors even if it’s not formally tracked. The question isn't just about privacy, but whether we're creating a system that punishes students for things outside their control.

For me, explainability (Q4) is key. I need to understand why the model thinks I’m struggling – ADHD means my study habits look different and could be misinterpreted. 

I went with ‘small’ on disability data because it *could* be useful if handled carefully, but only if fairness is prioritized. I agree about an opt-out, but also a way to challenge the model's assumptions about me personally.

Thanks everyone. I completely agree with S2 and A2 - Q3 felt like a slippery slope. As an advisor, I see students struggling *after* they’ve already fallen behind, and while early intervention is the goal, it needs to be done ethically. Absalon data feels particularly invasive; a marginal improvement isn't worth that level of tracking. 

I think Q4 – explainability – is absolutely vital. If I can’t articulate *why* a student has been flagged, how can I provide meaningful support? My responses reflected this, being stricter on needing improvements for lower explainability levels. I also strongly agree with the consensus around avoiding race/ethnicity and gender data. 

I'm slightly more open to considering first-generation status and financial aid – as an advisor, I see those systemic barriers constantly - but only with robust fairness safeguards. Perhaps focusing initial efforts on improving existing targeted outreach programs would be a less risky way forward?

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really challenging – especially with my dyslexia. It feels like even seemingly harmless data could be misinterpreted and unfairly impact me. The Absalon data felt like a definite overstep; it’s already stressful enough managing deadlines *with* extra time, without feeling watched.

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely critical. I need to understand *why* the model flagged me, and have a way to correct any misinterpretations about my learning style. My answers reflected that – I wouldn't accept lower explainability even for significant improvements in accuracy. I agree with the consensus on avoiding sensitive data like race and gender - those feel completely irrelevant and potentially harmful. An opt-out is essential, but also clear communication of *what*’s being tracked and why.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said – Q3 was incredibly difficult. As someone who dropped out once and then restarted, I’m acutely aware how easily things can spiral, but also how important it is to feel in control. The Absalon data felt like too much, even for a small improvement; it feels…surveilled.

I think explainability (Q4) is vital. Knowing *why* the model flagged me would be essential – as someone from the Faroe Islands adapting to a new system, my patterns might look different. I leaned towards ‘small’ on nationality and first-generation status because those experiences *do* shape access to support, but fairness must come first. Maybe strengthening existing culturally sensitive outreach could be a better starting point than building this model.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really unsettling – particularly given I *did* drop out of higher education once before. It feels like the system is already stacked against students who stumble, and adding more data points just amplifies that. Absalon data felt like a definite overreach; even a ‘small’ improvement doesn’t justify that level of tracking.

I think Q4 – explainability – is hugely important. As an EU national learning Danish, my study patterns might be different, so I need to understand *why* I'm flagged. My answers reflected that caution regarding sensitive data like nationality and financial aid; small improvements aren’t worth the risk without strong safeguards. An opt-out is vital, but even better would be proactive support for students adjusting to a new language and system.

Thanks everyone. I agree with much of what’s been said – Q3 really highlighted the tension between wanting to help students proactively and respecting their privacy. As an advisor for six years, I see students *after* they've struggled, so early identification is appealing, but Absalon data felt a step too far. 

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely crucial. We need to be able to articulate the ‘why’ behind any flag, to build trust and provide targeted support. My answers reflected that – I was stricter about needing improvement for lower levels of explainability. The divergence on nationality/financial aid shows these factors *do* impact access, but fairness must be paramount. Strengthening existing outreach alongside this model might be a good approach.

Thanks everyone, it’s really helpful to hear all those perspectives. I found Q3 very challenging – especially coming here as an international student myself this year. It felt like a lot of that data could easily be misinterpreted given the differences in educational systems and cultural expectations back home.

I think explainability (Q4) is incredibly important, even more so for someone adjusting to a new environment. Knowing *why* I’m flagged allows me to understand if it's genuinely a struggle or simply a difference in how things are done here. My answers reflected that caution – I prioritized clear explanations over small gains in accuracy. The consensus on avoiding sensitive data is reassuring, and an opt-out feels vital for building trust.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 incredibly difficult – balancing support with privacy felt really precarious. As someone managing a long-term health condition impacting my studies *and* being an international student, I’m hyper-aware of how easily data can be misinterpreted. Absalon data feels like a massive overstep; small improvements aren't worth that level of surveillance when you already feel ‘different’. 

For me, explainability (Q4) is vital. It's not enough to identify a problem – I need to understand *why* the model flagged me, given my circumstances might look unusual. My responses reflected that; even small gains weren’t worth sacrificing clear explanations. An opt-out is critical, but proactive transparency about data use would be better still.
